The Anatolian Indo-European language of second-millennium-BCE Anatolia, Hittite's closest well-attested kin and by some arguments the majority speech of the Hittite realm. This code is its cuneiform face — Luwian passages and incantations embedded in the tablet archives of Hattusa — as against the hieroglyphic Luwian of the seals and Iron Age monuments. The library holds it where it actually lives, inside the Hittite corpus: TLHdig's KBo/KUB tablets with Luwian content (206 documents, 3,604 passages, cited by CTH number), a few CDLI entries, and IE-CoR's cognate variety below.

Language of the Elymians of western Sicily (Segesta, Eryx), ~6th-4th c. BCE, Greek letters; almost entirely brief potsherd graffiti and coin legends. Machine-readable home: isicily (319 records, 267 with some edited text).
probably Indo-European; affiliation contested (Italic and Anatolian both proposed)

The bulk of attested Elymian: the language of the Elymians of western Sicily (Segesta, Eryx), ~6th–4th centuries BCE, written in Greek letters — almost entirely brief potsherd graffiti and coin legends, whose classification (Italic? Anatolian? honestly unresolved) rests on onomastics and a few case endings. This lane holds I.Sicily's Greek-script Elymian passages, 368 of them, the largest machine-readable body of the language anywhere and the epigraphic mass behind the xly code here. The -Grek subtag is ISO 15924 from each record's textLang/@mainLang; the xly base dossier covers the language, xly-Latn the editions' transliteration lane.
probably Indo-European; affiliation contested (Italic and Anatolian both proposed)

The editions' lane, not an ancient one: I.Sicily's transliteration siblings render Greek-script Elymian carvings line-for-line in Latin letters, and those -translit documents carry the xly-Latn tag — 9 passages across four records. Elymian, the contested-affiliation language of Segesta and Eryx in western Sicily, was never written in the Latin alphabet; the subtag marks the script of the rendering, carried honestly from each layer's textLang. The language is covered at xly, the carved Greek-script originals under xly-Grek.
Median (xme-old) and the Central-Iranian "Kermanic" dialect cluster Wiktionary files under xme-* (Old Azari, Hamadani…).

The unwritten Northwestern Iranian language of the Median confederacy, recoverable from personal names, Herodotean glosses and loanwords embedded in Old Persian royal vocabulary. Wiktionary files it as a variety under its Median code. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

The Malay creole of Manado and Minahasa in northern Sulawesi, thick with Dutch, Portuguese and Spanish loans and future-marking from local languages. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

Manichaean Middle Persian is Middle Persian — the Southwestern Iranian language of the Sasanian empire and ancestor of New Persian — as written in the clear Manichaean script of the Turfan manuscripts, the literature of Mani's church in Central Asia. The ISO code covers precisely that corpus, free of the archaizing heterograms that make Zoroastrian Pahlavi so opaque; the cognate data filed here stands for Middle Persian at large. On this library's shelves it appears through the etymology desk — cognate sets and reflex edges beside its Iranian relatives.

Anglo-Norman is the French of medieval England — the langue d'oïl the conquerors of 1066 brought across the Channel, which remained the language of the English court, law and much literature into the 15th century and salted English with thousands of French words. Fossil phrases of its 'law French' survive in English legal usage to this day. On this library's shelves it appears through the etymology desk — cognate sets and reflex edges beside its Romance relatives.

The language of ancient Phrygia, recorded in Old Phrygian inscriptions from the 8th century BCE and Neo-Phrygian curse formulas of Roman date; ancient and modern opinion places it close to Greek. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

Language of early-medieval northern Scotland, attested mostly in short ogham-script inscriptions and names; most now class it as Brittonic Celtic. Held: 12 documents (20 passages) from OG(H)AM — Ogham in 3D — the Scottish/Pictish ogham stones — plus 7 reflex edges.

One OG(H)AM-corpus document: the roman-letter reading of the Fordoun stone, Kincardineshire (s-kcd-002-roman) — Pictish in Latin letters, the -Latn lane beside the 12 stones of xpi-Ogam. Script subtag straight from the edition div's xml:lang, per the shelf's per-script layer-document convention.

The oghams of eastern Scotland that upstream does commit to Pictish (ISO 639-3 xpi): 12 OG(H)AM-corpus layer documents. The -Ogam subtag marks the genuine ogham layer per the shelf convention; the hesitant remainder of the Scottish series sits under und-Ogam, and the one roman-letter Pictish reading under xpi-Latn.

Parthian is the Northwestern Iranian language of the Arsacid empire, attested in the ostraca of Nisa, in inscriptions of the early Sasanian kings, and above all in the Manichaean manuscripts from Turfan, where it lived on as a church language long after it ceased to be spoken. Its deepest mark is indirect: a great share of the inherited vocabulary of Armenian is Parthian loanwords. On this library's shelves it appears through the etymology desk — cognate sets and reflex edges beside its Iranian relatives.

Western Phoenician of Carthage and its sphere, surviving into Roman North Africa as Neo-Punic. Held: 67 I.Sicily documents — funerary epitaphs and votive stelae from Sicily — largely catalogue records, with only a single transliterated passage so far. Eastern Phoenician is shelved as phn.

Punic — the western Phoenician of Carthage and its sphere — written in Greek letters, a marginal but real phenomenon of the Greek-Punic contact zones (Greco-Punic texts turn up where the two worlds mixed, and late Punic is elsewhere attested in both Greek and Latin dress). In this library the lane is a single I.Sicily passage (ISic020436) whose edition tags the text Punic in Greek script. The -Grek subtag is ISO 15924 from the record's textLang/@mainLang; the xpu base dossier covers Sicilian Punic, and xpu-Latn holds the editions' Latin-script renderings.

I.Sicily's Punic as the editions print it: the Semitic text of the island's Punic inscriptions rendered in Latin-script consonantal transliteration (mgn, ʿbdmlqrt…), 27 passages across a dozen records — funerary epitaphs, a votive to Astarte, an abecedarium, graffiti on Attic cups. The tag marks the script of the rendering, not an ancient writing habit: genuinely Latin-alphabet Punic (Latino-Punic) is a phenomenon of Roman North Africa, not of these Sicilian stones. The language — western Phoenician, surviving into Roman times as Neo-Punic — is covered at the xpu base dossier, with the lone Greek-script passage under xpu-Grek.

Old South Arabian language of the kingdom of Qatabān (Yemen, 1st millennium BCE), written in the musnad alphabet. A trace holding: 11 CDLI catalogue records of inscribed objects (Yale Babylonian Collection, YBC series) with no transliterated passages yet.
Tyrsenian (with Etruscan and Lemnian, per Rix 1998; non-Indo-European)

Language of the eastern Alps, ~6th-1st c. BCE, North Italic (Sanzeno/Magre) alphabets; short rock and bone inscriptions, many undecipherable. Corpus of record: tir (Thesaurus Inscriptionum Raeticarum, 389 inscriptions).
The steppe-Iranian branch: Proto-Scythian (xsc-pro), Proto-Saka (xsc-sak-pro), Proto-Sarmatian (xsc-sar-pro) — Ossetic's ancestry.

The extinct West Baltic language of the Yotvingians of the Suwałki-Grodno borderlands, close to Old Prussian and known from names, glosses and the disputed 'Pogańske gwary z Narewu' word list. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

The Continental Celtic of Gaul, attested from about the 3rd century BCE into the Roman era — dedications, graffiti, spindle-whorl mottoes and curse tablets, written first in Greek letters in the Mediterranean south, later in Latin ones — before Latin swallowed it entirely, leaving its trace as the substrate under French. The library's Gaulish is RIIG's epigraphic corpus, split by carved script into the lanes xtg-Grek (the Gallo-Greek majority), xtg-Latn and xtg-Lat, with Georges Dottin's La langue gauloise (1918) on the local shelf as grammar, texts and glossary (380 passages), and IE-CoR's cognate variety below.

RIIG's majority lane: 402 Gallo-Greek inscriptions — Transalpine Gaulish written in the Greek alphabet, the epigraphy of southern Gaul before Latin letters took over. The -Grek subtag is ISO 15924 straight from each file's textLang/@mainLang; the Latin-script sibling is xtg-Latn, and the xtg base dossier covers the language itself.

A one-monument lane: the Pilier d'Argentomagus (RIIG IND-01-01, from Saint-Marcel in the Indre; 8 passages), Transalpine Gaulish written in Latin letters, whose TEI textLang spells the script subtag "Lat" where its sibling files write ISO 15924 "Latn". The RIIG parser carries each file's tag whole rather than silently correcting it, so this spelling variant stands as its own lane beside xtg-Latn's 19 normalized Gallo-Latin inscriptions. The language — the Continental Celtic of Gaul, attested from the 3rd century BCE into the Roman era — is covered at the xtg base dossier, with the Greek-alphabet majority under xtg-Grek.

RIIG's Gallo-Latin lane: 19 inscriptions of Transalpine Gaulish written in Latin letters (Néris-les-Bains, the Ventabren stele…), the Roman-era counterpart to the Greek-alphabet majority under xtg-Grek. Script subtag from each file's textLang/@mainLang, per the RIIG parser convention; the xtg base dossier covers the language.

Tocharian A is the eastern of the two Tocharian languages, the easternmost branch of Indo-European, attested in Buddhist texts from Agni (Yanqi) and Turfan in the Tarim Basin of roughly the 5th-10th centuries CE, written in the same Brahmi-derived script as its sister. By the manuscript era it appears to have been a liturgical language kept up by monks whose everyday speech was Tocharian B or Uyghur. On this library's shelves it appears through the etymology desk — cognate sets and reflex edges beside its Indo-European relatives.

The Sabellic Italic language of ancient Umbria, Oscan's northern sibling, written in both a native Etruscan-derived alphabet and Latin letters. It is dominated by a single extraordinary monument: the Iguvine Tables of Gubbio, seven bronze tablets of ritual prescriptions for a priestly brotherhood — the longest text in any Sabellic language and the most detailed liturgical document surviving from pre-Roman Italy. The library holds exactly that center: CEIPoM's 68 Umbrian texts with the Tables sectioned tablet by tablet in both alphabets, the Wiktionary-derived Umbrian lexicon, and the shelf of Latin words borrowed from Umbrian.

Cuneiform state language of the kingdom of Urartu around Lake Van, 9th–7th centuries BCE; Hurrian's only known relative. Held: 699 texts from Oracc's eCUT (Electronic Corpus of Urartian Texts), gold-lemmatized with 15,961 rows, plus 4 CDLI entries — 703 documents, 6,129 passages.

The language of the pre-Roman Veneto (Este, Padua), 6th–1st c. BCE, written in a native alphabet derived from Etruscan. Its position within Indo-European is debated — most often grouped with (or beside) Italic; recorded here under Italic per that majority reading, honestly flagged.

Kamviri is the speech of the Kom people of Nuristan in northeastern Afghanistan and the adjacent Chitral border, usually classed as a dialect of Kamkata-viri beside Kati. It belongs to the Nuristani branch, the small third limb of Indo-Iranian, whose languages went essentially unrecorded before the 20th century. On this library's shelves it appears through the etymology desk — cognate sets and reflex edges beside its Indo-Iranian relatives.

The East Germanic of the Vandals, carried through Spain to Carthage, known only from names and a few phrases such as the 'froia arme' of a Latin epigram; it vanished with the kingdom in the 6th century. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

The Sabellic language of the Volsci of southern Latium, chiefly attested in the four-line Tabula Veliterna from Velitrae, sitting close to Umbrian within Italic. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.
unclassified (Tibeto-Burman sphere; the Bon tradition's sacred language)

The language of the Zhangzhung kingdom of western Tibet, known almost entirely from Bon religious texts and a handful of Dunhuang-period documents; its affiliation within Tibeto-Burman is debated. Held: the five OZ documents among OTDO's critical editions — upstream's own attribution, carried honestly.

Yaghnobi is the living descendant of a dialect of Sogdian, spoken by several thousand people from the remote Yaghnob valley of Tajikistan — a last echo of the Silk Road's great trade language. The community was forcibly resettled to the cotton lowlands in the 1970s, and only some families have since returned to the valley. On this library's shelves it appears through the etymology desk — cognate sets and reflex edges beside its Iranian relatives.

Yaqui is a Cahitan language of the Uto-Aztecan family, spoken along the Río Yaqui in Sonora, Mexico, and in Yaqui communities of Arizona, with centuries of Spanish contact. Held as the WOLD Yaqui vocabulary (Zarina Estrada Fernández; Haspelmath & Tadmor eds. 2009) — loanword-status and donor-language evidence at the etym desk.

The Pamir language of the Lutkoh valley in Chitral, Pakistan, twin of Munji across the Afghan border, together continuing an eastern Iranian line close to the extinct Bactrian. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

The language of Ashkenazi Jewry, a Middle High German-derived fusion written in Hebrew script with large Hebrew-Aramaic and Slavic components, carried from the Rhineland across Eastern Europe and the world. Its classic modern literature runs from Mendele and Sholem Aleichem to Singer's Nobel Prize. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

The Forth and Bargy dialect of County Wexford, Ireland — an offshoot of medieval English that survived in isolation until the mid-19th century, keeping archaisms lost everywhere else. A small literature of songs and glossaries preserves it, and a revival movement curates its remains. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists, in numbers out of all proportion to its tiny corpus.

The Yue Chinese of Guangzhou, Hong Kong and the worldwide Chinatown diaspora, preserving Middle Chinese final stops and a six-tone system that make it a key witness for reconstructing older Chinese; the library's ltc and och dossiers hold those ancestors. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

The dialect chain of the Zeeland islands and Goeree-Overflakkee, between Hollandic and West Flemish, keeping distinctions such as umlautless long vowels that standard Dutch has lost. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.
The ISO 639-1 alias of zho — see that dossier; Wiktionary descendant lists arrive under this two-letter form.

The generic ISO 639 macro-code for Chinese, used here not for texts but for the CJK writing-system apparatus: Unihan, the Unicode Han Database (102,998 entries), and BabelStone IDS, Ideographic Description Sequences for CJK ideographs (97,680 entries). Actual Sinitic holdings are shelved under lzh (Literary Chinese), och, ltc and cmn.

The Rus' branch and its historical stages — Old Novgorodian (zle-ono), Old Ruthenian (zle-ort), Middle Russian (zle-mru), Middle Belarusian/Ukrainian (zle-mbe, zle-muk) — modern be/ru/uk. The corpus's orv shelf sits here.

The stage of Belarusian within the Ruthenian chancery and literary tradition of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, roughly the 15th–18th centuries, before the modern standard was rebuilt on the living dialects. Wiktionary files it as an etymology-only stage. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.
The Muscovite stage between Old East Slavic and the modern standard (ca. 1400–1700) — Avvakum's era; held under orv per the UD convention.

The Ukrainian of roughly the 15th–18th centuries, continuous with the Ruthenian written language of the Polish-Lithuanian era, between Old East Slavic and the modern standard founded on Kotliarevsky and Shevchenko. Wiktionary files it as an etymology-only stage. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.
The birchbark-letter dialect of medieval Novgorod and Pskov (11th–15th c.), famously missing the second palatalization; attested in the corpus inside the orv birchbark shelf.

The medieval East Slavic dialect of Pskov, close kin to Old Novgorodian and like it preserving features outside the Kievan mainstream, known from chronicles and legal texts such as the Pskov Judicial Charter. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

The chancery and literary language of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Polish–Lithuanian east (14th–18th c., "prosta mova") — ancestor of Belarusian, Ukrainian, and Rusyn. The corpus holds its texts under orv (the UD convention).
OCS's own branch: Church Slavonic recensions (zls-chs), Slovenian, Serbo-Croatian, Bulgarian, Macedonian. The corpus's chu and sl shelves sit here.

The later, regionally recensioned continuation of Old Church Slavonic that served as the liturgical and learned language of Orthodox Slavdom and Romania into the modern era, leaving deep lexical strata in Russian and its neighbours. Wiktionary distinguishes it from the classical language of the first translations, which holds this library's cu dossier. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.
Polish, Czech, Slovak, Sorbian and their historical stages — Old Polish (zlw-opl), Middle Polish (zlw-mpl), Old Czech (zlw-ocs), Old Slovak (zlw-osk), Slovincian (zlw-slv).
Polish of ca. 1500–1780 (the print era between Old Polish and the modern standard).

The Czech of roughly the 12th–16th centuries, from the earliest glosses through the rich medieval literature of legends, chronicles and the Hussite writings that fixed much of the later standard. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists as the stage linking Proto-Slavic to modern Czech.
Polish to ca. 1500 — the stage Wiktionary's Proto-Slavic descendants cite most for Lechitic; no corpus texts held.

The medieval and early modern Slovak attested in Latin-context glosses, town books and pre-standard writings before Bernolák's and Štúr's codifications. Wiktionary files it as an etymology-only stage. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

The extinct westernmost Pomeranian Slavic of the Lake Łebsko fishermen, a sibling of Kashubian with free-stress archaisms, documented by Lorentz before it yielded to German in the early 20th century. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

South Africa's largest home language, an Nguni Bantu tongue with Khoisan-derived clicks and a written literature since the mid-19th century. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.

Kumzari is a Southwestern Iranian language spoken by the fishing community of Kumzar at the tip of Oman's Musandam peninsula on the Strait of Hormuz, and by the Shihuh nearby — the only Iranian language native to the Arabian Peninsula. Isolated among Arabic speakers, it is deeply mixed with Arabic and considered endangered. On this library's shelves it appears through the etymology desk — cognate sets and reflex edges beside its Iranian relatives.

The ISO "no linguistic content" tag: 592 CDLI records whose object carries no language — physical seals catalogued for their imagery ("CDLI Seals … (physical)") and uninscribed or anepigraphic tablets. The CDLI adapter mints it from ATF's "nlc" and the catalog values "no linguistic content"/"uninscribed"; genuinely unknown languages go to und instead.

The Northwestern Iranian language of the Zazas in eastern Anatolia, kin to Gorani and historically to the Caspian languages rather than to the Kurdish that surrounds it; written use has grown since the 1980s diaspora. It reaches this library through the etymology desk's cognate lists.
